Mohit, you asked how Kunal, the kid who never studied, jumped from sixty-eight in the unit test. I'll tell you the whole thing.
I wanted ninety in physics finals. So I sat with last year's paper. Seventy marks theory. Mechanics carries about twenty-three, electricity about eighteen, optics fourteen, and so on. I asked myself, where am I losing? Mechanics I'm fine. Electricity I was getting maybe half.
Then I counted weeks. Exam's on the fourth of March, which gave me eleven weeks. Electricity has four chapters, so that's one chapter every week for four weeks, twenty numericals each. Then optics, three weeks. Then four weeks of full papers.
Every Sunday night I checked: did I hit twenty? Twice I didn't, so the next week was twenty-five.
Honestly, the number ninety scared me. Twenty problems a week didn't.

qa.q: How many weeks did Kunal have before the exam?
qa.a: Kunal had eleven weeks before the exam on the fourth of March.

qa.q: Why did the weekly target of twenty problems feel better to Kunal than the goal of ninety?
qa.a: The goal of ninety made Kunal feel scared, but twenty problems a week felt manageable and gave a sense of control.

qa.q: What else could Kunal do if two weeks fell short, and why?
qa.a: Kunal could ask a teacher to check which kinds of numericals keep going wrong, so extra practice goes where marks are really lost.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Kunal's weekly plan?
qa.a: Mohit may find it surprising and useful, since the jump from sixty-eight came from clear weekly counts rather than just working harder.

I'm Varun, Anjali Didi's younger brother, and I share a wall with her room, so I heard all of this.
Last Sunday she spread her physics syllabus on the floor and started talking to herself. "Ninety out of hundred. Practicals are thirty, I'll get twenty-eight. So I need sixty-two out of seventy in theory."
Then she took the marks per unit from the board paper. "Waves and optics, fourteen. I'm weakest there. Rotation, I'm fine."
She counted on the calendar. "Exam's in fourteen weeks. Optics first, one chapter a week, thirty problems."
Now there's a chart taped to her cupboard with every week in a box. On Sunday nights she ticks it and mutters numbers. I don't know if she's nervous or calm. She hums while she does it, though.

qa.q: How many marks does Anjali say she needs in theory?
qa.a: She says she needs sixty-two out of seventy in theory.

qa.q: What might Anjali's humming while she ticks the chart suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she feels calmer and more in control now that the big goal is broken into weekly boxes, though the observer can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Anjali add to her weekly boxes, and why?
